Credit Card Customer Churn: Who Leaves, Why, and What Should We Do?¶

Business question: Which customers are leaving, why, and which segment should receive which retention action, and is it worth the money?

Data: Kaggle Credit Card Customers (BankChurners.csv): 10,127 retail credit-card customers, 16% attrition.

Approach: data audit and missing-data strategy → EDA → hypothesis tests (chi-square, t-test) → interpretable models (logistic regression vs. shallow decision tree) → behavioral segments → USD campaign business case with scenarios.

The goal is not model accuracy. It is findings and a decision: what to do, for whom, and what it is worth.

Cleaning decisions

Column(s) Decision Why
Naive_Bayes_Classifier_... (2 cols) Drop Pre-computed outputs of someone else's classifier of the target. Keeping them is target leakage.
CLIENTNUM Drop (keep as index) Identifier, no signal.
Avg_Open_To_Buy Drop Equals Credit_Limit − Total_Revolving_Bal (verified below), so it is redundant.
Attrition_Flag Encode as churn (1 = attrited) Target.

1.1 Missing-data strategy¶

There are no NaNs, but Unknown is hidden missing data in three columns. Before choosing a strategy I check whether the missingness is informative (does churn differ for Unknown rows?) and how much is affected.

In [4]:
miss_cols = ["Education_Level", "Marital_Status", "Income_Category"]
rows = []
for c in miss_cols:
    unk = df[c].eq("Unknown")
    ct = pd.crosstab(unk, df.churn)
    p = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)[1]
    rows.append({"column": c, "unknown_share": unk.mean(), "churn_unknown": df.loc[unk, "churn"].mean(),
                 "churn_known": df.loc[~unk, "churn"].mean(), "p_value": p})
miss = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("column")
print("Rows with at least one Unknown:", f"{(df[miss_cols] == 'Unknown').any(axis=1).mean():.1%}")
miss.style.format({"unknown_share": "{:.1%}", "churn_unknown": "{:.1%}", "churn_known": "{:.1%}", "p_value": "{:.3f}"})

Rows with at least one Unknown: 30.1%
Out[4]:
  unknown_share churn_unknown churn_known p_value
column        
Education_Level 15.0% 16.9% 15.9% 0.385
Marital_Status 7.4% 17.2% 16.0% 0.398
Income_Category 11.0% 16.8% 16.0% 0.497

Finding: see the p-values above: churn does not differ meaningfully between Unknown and known rows, so missingness looks uninformative. Dropping the ~30% of rows with any Unknown would waste data and shrink the churner sample.

Strategy: keep Unknown as its own category (no invented values) and verify the choice with a sensitivity check against two alternatives: dropping rows and mode-imputation.

In [5]:
def build_pre(cat_cols, num_cols, refs):
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop=refs, handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols),
        ("num", StandardScaler(), num_cols)])

REFS = {"Gender": "F", "Education_Level": "Graduate", "Marital_Status": "Married",
        "Income_Category": "Less than $40K", "Card_Category": "Blue"}
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)

def cv_auc(data):
    X, y = data[CAT + NUM], data.churn
    refs = [REFS[c] if REFS[c] in data[c].unique() else None for c in CAT]
    pipe = Pipeline([("pre", build_pre(CAT, NUM, refs)), ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000))])
    p = cross_val_predict(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
    return roc_auc_score(y, p)

known = df[~(df[miss_cols] == "Unknown").any(axis=1)]
imputed = df.copy()
for c in miss_cols:
    imputed[c] = imputed[c].replace("Unknown", imputed.loc[imputed[c] != "Unknown", c].mode()[0])

sens = pd.Series({"Unknown as category (chosen)": cv_auc(df),
                  "Drop rows with Unknown": cv_auc(known),
                  "Mode imputation": cv_auc(imputed)}, name="CV ROC-AUC").round(4)
RESULTS["missing_sensitivity"] = sens.to_dict()
sens.to_frame()
Out[5]:
CV ROC-AUC
Unknown as category (chosen) 0.9238
Drop rows with Unknown 0.9182
Mode imputation 0.9237

The three strategies give essentially the same AUC, so the choice is not material; "Unknown as category" keeps all rows and invents nothing.

3. Hypothesis tests¶

With n ≈ 10,000, almost anything is statistically significant, so each test reports an effect size (Cramér's V for chi-square; Cohen's d for t-tests) and p-values are Holm-corrected within each family. The question that matters is how big the difference is.

Headline hypotheses

  • H0: churn is independent of Card_Category / Months_Inactive_12_mon. H1: it is not. (chi-square)
  • H0: mean Total_Trans_Ct is equal for attrited vs. existing customers. H1: it differs. (Welch t-test, with Mann-Whitney as a non-parametric check)
In [10]:
test_df = df.copy()
test_df["Card_Category"] = test_df["Card_Category"].replace({"Gold": "Gold/Platinum", "Platinum": "Gold/Platinum"})  # Platinum n=20 -> expected counts too small
cat_tests = CAT + ["Dependent_count", "Total_Relationship_Count", "Months_Inactive_12_mon", "Contacts_Count_12_mon"]
rows = []
for c in cat_tests:
    ct = pd.crosstab(test_df[c], test_df.churn)
    chi2, p, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2 / ct.values.sum() / (min(ct.shape) - 1))
    rows.append({"feature": c, "chi2": chi2, "dof": dof, "p_value": p, "cramers_v": v, "min_expected_count": exp.min()})
chi = pd.DataFrame(rows)
chi["p_holm"] = multipletests(chi.p_value, method="holm")[1]
chi["effect"] = pd.cut(chi.cramers_v, [0, .1, .3, .5, 1], labels=["negligible", "small", "medium", "large"])
chi = chi.sort_values("cramers_v", ascending=False).set_index("feature")
RESULTS["chi_square"] = chi[["cramers_v", "p_holm"]].round(4).to_dict("index")
chi.style.format({"chi2": "{:.1f}", "p_value": "{:.2e}", "p_holm": "{:.2e}", "cramers_v": "{:.3f}", "min_expected_count": "{:.1f}"}) \
   .background_gradient(subset=["cramers_v"], cmap="Reds")

DISCRETE = ["Dependent_count", "Total_Relationship_Count", "Months_Inactive_12_mon", "Contacts_Count_12_mon"]
rows = []
for c in NUM:
    if c in DISCRETE:
        continue
    a, b = df.loc[df.churn == 1, c], df.loc[df.churn == 0, c]
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
    u, pu = stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided")
    d = (a.mean() - b.mean()) / np.sqrt((a.var() + b.var()) / 2)
    rows.append({"feature": c, "mean_attrited": a.mean(), "mean_existing": b.mean(), "cohens_d": d, "p_welch": p, "p_mannwhitney": pu})
tt = pd.DataFrame(rows)
tt["p_holm"] = multipletests(tt.p_welch, method="holm")[1]
tt["effect"] = pd.cut(tt.cohens_d.abs(), [0, .2, .5, .8, 10], labels=["negligible", "small", "medium", "large"])
tt = tt.reindex(tt.cohens_d.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index).set_index("feature")
RESULTS["t_tests"] = tt[["mean_attrited", "mean_existing", "cohens_d", "p_holm"]].round(4).to_dict("index")
tt.style.format({"mean_attrited": "{:,.2f}", "mean_existing": "{:,.2f}", "cohens_d": "{:.2f}", "p_welch": "{:.1e}", "p_mannwhitney": "{:.1e}", "p_holm": "{:.1e}"}) \
  .background_gradient(subset=["cohens_d"], cmap="RdBu", vmin=-1.3, vmax=1.3)

What the tests say (numbers in the tables above)

  1. Behavior dominates; demographics barely matter on their own (marginal tests). Gender, education, marital status, income, card tier and dependents all have negligible effect sizes (Cramér's V < 0.1). Contacts, inactivity and number of products have noticeably larger effects.
  2. The biggest gaps are in transaction behavior: transaction count (a large effect), the Q4/Q1 change in transaction count, revolving balance, utilization and spend. Age, tenure and credit limit are negligible even where p < 0.05.
  3. Practical implication: campaigns should be targeted on behavioral triggers, not on demographic profiles.
  4. Caveat: transaction measures are computed over the same 12 months in which customers left, so part of the gap is churners already disengaging. That makes these features early-warning signals rather than root causes (see limitations).

4. Models: logistic regression vs. decision tree¶

Both are interpretable on purpose. I use 5-fold stratified cross-validation, no class re-weighting (so predicted probabilities stay calibrated for the cost/benefit step), and a business-friendly metric: the share of all churners captured in the top 20% of customers ranked by risk.

In [12]:
X, y = df[CAT + NUM], df.churn
refs = [REFS[c] for c in CAT]
def lr_pipe(): return Pipeline([("pre", build_pre(CAT, NUM, refs)), ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000))])
def tree_pipe(depth=4): return Pipeline([("pre", build_pre(CAT, NUM, refs)),
                                         ("m", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=50, random_state=SEED))])

def top_share(y, p, frac=.2):
    k = int(len(y) * frac); idx = np.argsort(-p)[:k]
    return y.values[idx].sum() / y.sum()

oof = {}
for name, pipe in [("Logistic regression", lr_pipe()), ("Decision tree (depth 4)", tree_pipe())]:
    oof[name] = cross_val_predict(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]

metrics = pd.DataFrame({n: {"ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y, p), "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y, p),
                            "Churners captured in top 20%": top_share(y, p),
                            "Precision @ p>0.5": ((p > .5) & (y == 1)).sum() / max((p > .5).sum(), 1),
                            "Recall @ p>0.5": ((p > .5) & (y == 1)).sum() / y.sum()} for n, p in oof.items()}).T
RESULTS["model_metrics"] = metrics.round(4).to_dict("index")
metrics.style.format("{:.3f}")
Out[12]:

Both models rank customers far better than random: the top 20% by risk contain most churners (table above). The logistic regression is well calibrated (right chart), which is what the dollar calculation in Section 6 needs. Because model comparison is not the goal, I use each model for what it does best: the logistic regression for effect directions and probabilities, the tree for readable rules.

4.1 What drives churn (odds ratios)¶

In [14]:
# statsmodels Logit for confidence intervals; numeric features standardised -> OR is "per +1 standard deviation"
Xd = pd.get_dummies(df[CAT], drop_first=False).astype(float)
Xd = Xd.drop(columns=[f"{c}_{r}" for c, r in REFS.items()])
Xn = (df[NUM] - df[NUM].mean()) / df[NUM].std()
Xs = sm.add_constant(pd.concat([Xd, Xn], axis=1))
logit = sm.Logit(y, Xs).fit(disp=0, maxiter=200)
orr = pd.DataFrame({"odds_ratio": np.exp(logit.params), "ci_low": np.exp(logit.conf_int()[0]),
                    "ci_high": np.exp(logit.conf_int()[1]), "p": logit.pvalues}).drop(index="const")
sig = orr[orr.p < 0.01].copy(); sig["abs_log"] = np.abs(np.log(sig.odds_ratio)); sig = sig.sort_values("abs_log", ascending=True).tail(12)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 5.2))
colors = [C_CHURN if v > 1 else C_STAY for v in sig.odds_ratio]
ax.hlines(range(len(sig)), sig.ci_low, sig.ci_high, color=colors, lw=2)
ax.scatter(sig.odds_ratio, range(len(sig)), color=colors, zorder=3)
ax.axvline(1, color="k", lw=1); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yticks(range(len(sig))); ax.set_yticklabels([i.replace("_", " ") for i in sig.index])
ax.set_xlabel("Odds ratio (log scale; numeric features per +1 SD; 95% CI)"); ax.set_title("Strongest churn drivers (logistic regression, p < 0.01)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / "06_odds_ratios.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
RESULTS["top_odds_ratios"] = sig.sort_values("abs_log", ascending=False)[["odds_ratio", "ci_low", "ci_high"]].round(3).to_dict("index")
sig.sort_values("abs_log", ascending=False)[["odds_ratio", "ci_low", "ci_high", "p"]].round(3)

Reading the odds ratios (directional, given the correlated features): values above 1 raise churn odds, below 1 lower them. Transaction count and the Q4/Q1 change in transaction count are protective; months inactive and contacts with the bank raise risk; holding more products is protective. Demographics: weak on their own, not zero once behavior is held constant. Section 3 showed negligible marginal effects, but in the multivariable model a few demographic terms remain noticeable (male customers lower, $120K+ income and single customers higher). Because they carry little ranking power on their own (see the tree and the effect sizes), I treat them as hypotheses for follow-up, not as targeting criteria.

Two cautions. (1) Total_Trans_Amt shows an odds ratio above 1 even though raw churners spend less: once transaction count is in the model, a higher amount means a higher average ticket, and the two features are strongly correlated (a sign-flip typical of multicollinearity). Read it as an artifact, not a business insight. (2) The Gold-card odds ratio rests on only 116 customers, so its confidence interval is wide.

The first splits are on transaction count, revolving balance, Q4/Q1 transaction change, product count and months inactive: the same behavioral signals, now as readable rules. These motivate the segments in the next section.

5. Behavioral segments and actions¶

Segments are rule-based (so a business team can apply them without a model), mutually exclusive (assigned in priority order), and each is tied to one action.

# Segment (rule) Hypothesised reason Proposed action
S1 Disengaging: Q4/Q1 transaction-count ratio < 0.5, or inactive ≥ 3 months with < 50 transactions Card is being abandoned Reactivation: spend-triggered cashback + early-warning alert
S2 Single-product, no revolving balance: ≤ 2 products and zero revolving balance Low switching cost, no relationship Relationship bundle: cross-sell a second product, fee/rate benefit
S3 Service friction: ≥ 4 contacts in 12 months Unresolved problems Service recovery: senior callback and root-cause fix
S4 High-value stable: top-quartile annual revenue, none of the above Competitor poaching Priority care: relationship-manager review
– Core: everyone else – No campaign (business as usual)
In [16]:
# --- Revenue proxy (the dataset has no revenue column, so assumptions are explicit) ---
ASSUMP = dict(
    interchange_rate = 0.018,    # share of card spend earned as interchange
    revolve_margin   = 0.15,     # net margin on revolving balance (APR minus funding and credit-loss cost)
    annual_fee       = {"Blue": 0, "Silver": 40, "Gold": 75, "Platinum": 150},
    contact_cost     = 2.0,      # USD per customer contacted (SMS / e-mail / outbound call mix)
    incentive        = 25.0,     # USD cashback per customer who accepts the offer
    redeem_nonchurn  = 0.20,     # share of contacted non-churners who also claim the incentive (cost leakage)
    save_rate        = 0.25,     # share of would-be churners retained by the campaign (to be validated by A/B test)
)
df["revenue"] = (ASSUMP["interchange_rate"] * df.Total_Trans_Amt + ASSUMP["revolve_margin"] * df.Total_Revolving_Bal
                 + df.Card_Category.map(ASSUMP["annual_fee"]))

6. Business case: what is it worth? (USD)¶

Mechanics (per contacted customer)

  • Cost: contact_cost for everyone contacted, plus incentive for every would-be churner who is saved and for non-churners who also claim the offer (deadweight cost, redeem_nonchurn).
  • Benefit: save_rate × (annual revenue of the churner − incentive), counted for one year only (conservative: a retained customer typically stays longer).
  • Revenue of a would-be churner is measured on their current (already depressed) activity, which is also conservative.

All monetary results are assumption-driven. The assumptions live in one dictionary (ASSUMP) so they can be replaced with the bank's real numbers. The save_rate is the key unknown and must be validated with an A/B test.

In [18]:
def econ(sub, A):
    N, C = len(sub), sub.churn.sum()
    vbar = sub.loc[sub.churn == 1, "revenue"].mean() if C else 0
    saved = A["save_rate"] * C
    benefit = saved * (vbar - A["incentive"])
    cost = N * A["contact_cost"] + (N - C) * A["redeem_nonchurn"] * A["incentive"]
    be = cost / (C * (vbar - A["incentive"])) if C and vbar > A["incentive"] else np.inf   # break-even save rate
    return dict(contacted=N, would_churn=int(C), saved=saved, benefit=benefit, cost=cost, net=benefit - cost, breakeven_save_rate=be)

rows = {s: econ(g, ASSUMP) for s, g in df.groupby("segment") if not s.startswith("Core")}
seg_econ = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
seg_econ["roi"] = seg_econ.net / seg_econ.cost
seg_econ = seg_econ.sort_values("net", ascending=False)
RESULTS["segment_economics"] = seg_econ.astype(float).round(3).to_dict("index")
seg_econ.style.format({"contacted": "{:,.0f}", "would_churn": "{:,.0f}", "saved": "{:,.0f}", "benefit": "${:,.0f}", "cost": "${:,.0f}",
                       "net": "${:,.0f}", "breakeven_save_rate": "{:.0%}", "roi": "{:.1%}"}) \
        .background_gradient(subset=["net"], cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-20000, vmax=20000)

How to read it: a blanket campaign pays only where churn is concentrated. Compare each segment's break-even save rate with the assumed 25%: segments above it lose money if contacted in full. That is why the final recommendation targets individuals with positive expected value, not whole segments.

6.1 Expected-value targeting¶

For each customer, contact only if the expected net of the campaign is positive, using the out-of-fold churn probability p from the (calibrated) logistic regression:

EV = p × save_rate × (revenue − incentive) − (1 − p) × redeem_nonchurn × incentive − contact_cost

This is a closed-form rule from the assumptions, with no threshold tuned on the data.

In [19]:
df["p_churn"] = oof["Logistic regression"]

def ev_plan(d, A):
    ev = (d.p_churn * A["save_rate"] * (d.revenue - A["incentive"])
          - (1 - d.p_churn) * A["redeem_nonchurn"] * A["incentive"] - A["contact_cost"])
    t = d[ev > 0]
    r = econ(t, A); r["share_of_churners_reached"] = t.churn.sum() / d.churn.sum()
    return r, t

plan, targeted = ev_plan(df, ASSUMP)
print(f"Contact {plan['contacted']:,.0f} of {len(df):,} customers ({plan['contacted']/len(df):.0%}); reach {plan['share_of_churners_reached']:.0%} of churners")
print(f"Expected saves: {plan['saved']:,.0f} customers | benefit ${plan['benefit']:,.0f} | cost ${plan['cost']:,.0f} | NET ${plan['net']:,.0f}/year | ROI {plan['net']/plan['cost']:.0%}")
print("\nWho gets contacted (by segment):")
print(targeted.groupby("segment").size().rename("targeted").to_frame().join(df.groupby("segment").size().rename("segment_size")).assign(share=lambda x: (x.targeted/x.segment_size).round(2)))
RESULTS["ev_plan"] = {k: float(v) for k, v in plan.items()}
RESULTS["ev_by_segment"] = targeted.groupby("segment").size().to_dict()

7. Limitations and next steps¶

  • Revenue is a proxy, built from interchange, revolving margin and annual fee under stated assumptions. Replace ASSUMP with real P&L data.
  • Save rate is the key unknown. Run an A/B test: randomly hold out ~10% of the targeted list as a control, and measure the incremental retention before scaling.
  • Features are measured in the same window as churn. Transaction decline is partly the symptom of leaving. For production, build the score on a lagged window (e.g., behavior in months 1–6 predicting churn in months 7–12) so it fires early enough to act.
  • Correlation, not causation. Segments tell us where churn concentrates, not that a given action causes retention; an uplift model is the logical follow-up.
  • One-year benefit horizon is deliberately conservative; multi-year customer lifetime value would raise the case.
  • Sample is a single anonymised portfolio; results are scaled linearly to larger books for illustration only.

Who is leaving? 16.1% of customers (1,627). The riskiest group, S1 Disengaging, is 23% of customers but 63% of churners (churn rate 45%, 2.8x average).

Why? Mostly behavior. On their own, demographic effect sizes are negligible (Cramér's V <= 0.04), while transaction count differs strongly between attrited and existing customers (Cohen's d = -1.24). Fewer products, more inactive months and repeated service contacts also raise risk.

What to do? Reactivation cashback for S1, relationship bundles for single-product customers, service recovery for repeat contactors, but only for customers whose expected value is positive (2,431 of 10,127 customers, 59% of churners reached).

What is it worth? Base case about $30,613 net per year for this 10,127-customer portfolio (about $3.0M per 1M customers). Range: $7,142 (10% save rate) to $49,091 (35% save rate). Validate the save rate with an A/B test before scaling.
